speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, may I crave your indulgence and the indulgence of the house for a moment to make a word of personal explanation with regard to a story concerning my personal plans which is being carried in many newspapers and which I am told was also the subject of comment last night over the radio. For instance, in the Montreal Gazette the story appears under this title:
St. Laurent to retire soon from public life.
Ottawa, May 21 (CP) -
I take that to mean the Canadian Press.
Justice Minister St. Laurent said to-day in an interview he plans to retire from public life shortly and return to the law practice he left in Quebec in 1941 to take the justice department portfolio for the war period.
I must say that I gave no such interview to the Canadian Press. The night before last I did have a conversation with a newspaper man and there is a paragraph in this which I certainly did authorize. The last paragraph reads:
He termed as "ridiculous" a newspaper report which said speculation among back-bench Liberals was to the effect that Prime Minister Mackenzie King would retire within a year, appoint Mr. St. Laurent to succeed him, and continue to sit as Liberal member for Glengarry until the next election, when he would retire.
Labour Conditions

I said that that was ridiculous and that I had no objection to being quoted as saying that. As to the preceding paragraphs about plans of mine to retire shortly from public life, I have given no interview about that, nor have I authorized the publication of any such statement. There are many newspaper men who have known ever since my first meeting with the press when I came to Ottawa as Minister of Justice in 1941 that I retained the hope of getting back at a convenient time to my law practice, but I have no definite plans that would warrant any announcement. I would not say anything about this except that the language used would appear to convey the impression that I had made a declaration about it for publication. Whenever these plans are sufficiently definite to warrant an announcement, that announcement probably will be made in a more formal manner than in the course of casual conversation with a friendly newspaper man.

speechtext: This question has been given a great deal of consideration. There are many complications in connection with it. The revised answer is:
The upward revision in the maximum prices of farm machinery, made effective April 13 by the board, constitutes provision for appropriate increases in prices, but does not make such increases mandatory.
In any case where a buyer and seller had a firm contract as of April 13 for future delivery of farm machinery at prices lower than the new maximum price, the buyer has the ordinary protection of law against any variation in the contract price, althpugh if both buyer and seller agree, the price might be adjusted within the limits of the revised maximum price.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott) I wish to oppose this motion on the ground that it is not in the public interest to produce such reports, and also that the report is privileged and therefore should not be produced. The hon. member on the 4th of April asked the minister when the report would be produced in the house, and he was then informed that it was not customary to produce such reports in the house and that this practice would be followed. This rule has been followed previously as regards docu-
Canadian Army in Holland

merits pertaining to military courts. The stand taken was that it was not in the public interest to produce such documentation because it would seriously hamper the administration of justice in the armed services if officers who in the course of duty are called upon to serve on these courts martial or to prepare such reports are made to feel that their actions or their statements may be debated in the House of Commons or be the subject of some controversy in this house. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that even more serious considerations exist as regards courts of inquiry. My hon. friend knows very well that courts of inquiry in the armed forces are an ordinary matter of administration, taking place every day; they are convened at the demand of the minister or of a commanding officer to inform this officer on any matter affecting the ordinary course of internal administration in the army or in the other services. As a matter of fact, the rules of procedure provided for under the Army Act state that such courts of inquiry and such reports are not admissible in evidence in courts martial which may follow; and I think it is very clear-*

subsubtopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I come from a constituency which contains all classes of people. It has the . white collar class, which has had fixed wages plus a cost of living bonus during the war; industrial workers employed in the great railway shops adjacent to Winnipeg; the mill workers in Selkirk; the fishermen on the lakes, and also the farmers. During the war all these people have been subject to prices fixed and controlled and maintained by the government. The advances in prices of farm machinery and steel have caused this debate.
I have listened patiently to all parties in the house offer their arguments, and the very thought of ceilings being broken and the spiral of inflation starting causes me a great deal of concern. I saw inflation at work when I came here as an immigrant in 1919.
I became a farmer in 1920 when everything was high, and about eighteen months afterwards, cattle I had purchased for S140 and $150 were worth only $25 or $30. Surely everyone of my age must know that the same thing will happen again if we allow our price ceilings and floors to disappear.
I come now to the implement companies. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has defended them and has told the house that they needed this advance. Personally I cannot see that they do. I notice from the papers of April, 1938, that the shares of Cockshutt Plow were quoted at 7 while the shares of Massey Harris were quoted at 5*.
I shall not give the quotations for the shares of other companies, as I think these two are sufficient for my purpose. By April 2 of this year the shares of Cockshutt Plow had advanced to 16| while those of Massey Harris had come up to 171. According to to-day's paper
there was a further increase, Cockshutt shares being quoted at 171 and Massey Harris at 18*.
I admit that I know more about live stock than this sort of stock, but it seems to me that these companies must be in a sound financial position when there is this improvement in the value of their shares on the stock market. These increases show that there must be an expectancy of greater profits in the future. I cannot go into details with the Minister of Finance in the same way as those who are trained in finance, but here is the way I look at it: No one would be buying these shares unless he thought there were to be greater profits than before. I cannot forget the report made in 1937 by a committee of this house. It contained thirty-six recommendations, but I shall refer only to three which appear on page 500. They are as follows:
28.	That the profit to the farm implement companies on the sale of replacement parts is excessive, and the price of these to the consumer should be materially reduced.
29.	That the increases announced by the companies in January, 1936, were not justified by an increase in manufacturing or distribution costs or by the financial results of the companies in so far as these were affected by the price level of farm implements.
30.	That over the period 1891-1936 retail prices of farm implements have been maintained at too high a level as shown by the financial returns to the companies engaged in the industry during that period.
I wonder if those things were taken into account when the machinery companies made their representations to the wartime prices and trade board. I have the gravest doubts about the increase that has been granted in the prices of farm machinery. The companies' case should have been made public, so that farmers, not only in the constituency of Selkirk but throughout the whole of Canada, could have read for themselves why it was thought that this price increase was justified.
When the leader of the Conservative party was the leader of the Liberal-Progressives in Manitoba he used to advance an argument with which I agreed. He maintained that as agriculturists made up one-third of the population they were entitled to one-third of the nation's income. I hope the leader of the opposition still holds that view.

subsubtopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: He still maintains the same argument.

subsubtopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that. I would point out to him that the only time agriculture ever came near to getting one-TRird of the national income was at the end of the last war, and since we have had the stabilization of floor and ceiling prices.
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

subsubtopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: They never received it in the history of the country.

subsubtopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I said that the only time they had come near to getting it was-at the end of the last war, when I came here from Scotland, and during this war. The other day the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) placed some figures on Hansard to show that we were a long way from getting one-third of the national income. Certain hon. members who sit behind the leader of the opposition have advanced the argument that price ceilings should be abandoned, that the lid should be taken off, that we should let things go. Surely no hon. member who has the support of a farming community can be in his senses when he makes that request.
The farmer has always been the victim of prices. When he has anything to Sfell, he must go to the packing house or some other organization and say, "How much will you give me for this?" When he wants to buy anything, he must go and say, "How much do you want for this?" He has had to buy in a controlled market and sell in a controlled market. The worker is in the same position. He must sell his labour in a controlled market, and he must buy the necessities of life in the same type of market. Perhaps when the worker and the farmer and the fisherman become better organized-labour is organized only about twenty per cent; the farmer about, the same and the fisherman much less-they will be able to combat big business, the manufacturers and the packing-houses which are all organized one hundred per cent. Even our lawyers and doctors are organized one hundred per cent.
The farmer does not want to hold up the consumer for unreasonable prices, but he must have his costs of production. Producing food for the nation must give a return to the farmer which will provide him with a standard of living equal to that enjoyed by other people. Guaranteed prices must be maintained over a period of years so that the farmer can look ahead and plan his production accordingly. The worker should have a guaranteed wage so that he will be able to budget' and plan for the future.
I should like to deal for a moment with the cattle situation. A great deal has been said in recent weeks about the shortage in the supply of cattle. Personally I do not think it has been so much a shortage of cattle. The shortage of supplies can be immediately traced back to the order of the wartime prices and trade board about two years ago fixing the price for cattle for the whole year round; that is, one price irrespective of when you
fMr. Bryce.]
marketed your cattle. In the cattle business you have to look fairly well ahead and arrange your business so when the order of the wartime prices and trade board was issued the farmers took some time to reorganize their plans.
This spring has shown a lack of supplies for the simple reason that it does not pay the farmer to feed cattle in the winter time.
One hon. member to my left said a few days ago that there was really no difference between grass-fed and stall-fed cattle. I cannot agree with his view, and in support of what I think is right, I submit that the packer in Canada has always been prepared to pay two cents more for stall-fed cattle. Surely every hon. member in this house, whether he has an agricultural background or not, must realize that the feeding of cattle in this country in the winter entails a great deal of work. Even if you do not take into consideration the feeding of grain, and you only .put the hay in front of the cattle and take it away from behind them, that entails a certain amount of lhbour that the man who markets grass-fed cattle does not have to do.
In discussing this wartime prices and trade board ruling on previous occasions with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), he has assured me that some farmers asked that the price be the same the year round. Of course I agree with him this far. If I were a rancher I would think that the Minister of Agriculture was a fine fellow, or if I were a farmer in Ontario with a few grass farms and I could buy cattle in the spring and put them on that grass, I would think the minister was a fine fellow too. But I am thinking of the man who puts in steers in the fall and feeds them through until the spring. He certainly deserves a greater return for his labour.
Coming back to the man who has been in the habit of feeding steers through the winter, there is no incentive whatever for the extra feed or the extra labour involved, and this, might I point out to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, is one policy of the wartime prices and trade board previously made was steady supply of meat every month of the year. The arrangement which the wartime prices and trade board that is hindering a in my estimation on a much fairer basis, because the farmer was encouraged to feed cattle during the winter and market them during the spring months when our shortest supply comes, but under the present policy he can market his cattle any time and they must still sell at one and the same price.

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
Now that we are beginning to reap the fruits of the present policy of the wartime prices and trade board in this regard we can expect a flooded market this fall, when the packers-will not be able to absorb the heavy run and will bid a lower price. The packer will sit back and dominate the situation and instead of the farmer getting 12 cents for his steer, as he is entitled to according to the wartime prices and trade board, he will no doubt have to take 10J or 11 cents.
Of course I know that the minister is going to tell me that the meat board will come on the market and buy up these cattle and have them processed so that the farmer will not have to take a loss. But might I remind the minister that the packing companies cannot process what they have now; so where is the government going to have them processed?
This brings me back to a previous argument I made in the house, which is that the only ceiling or floor on cattle to-day is after they are hung up by the heels in the packing plant. The live animal is never taken into consideration; there is neither a ceiling nor a floor to protect the farmer when he sells his animals on the hoof. It is only after they are dead that the ceilings begin to apply.
The Minister of Agriculture told us last week that the subsidy to the consumer of milk is to be removed. This just throws the prob-' lem right back into the lap of the provincial milk boards. The removal of the subsidy and the resulting increase in the cost of milk to the consumer can result in either of two things-an increase in the cost of living index, or a lowering of the consumption of milk. Milk is the most necessary item in our diet. Research carried on by the medical profession, the army, air force, and navy, has proved conclusively that milk is something everyone should have. I therefore deplore the discontinuance of the subsidy on milk, both from the nutritional standpoint and because it will raise the cost of living. It will strike at the old-age pensioner and at all people of limited means-the widows, for instance, who have lost their husbands in this war, because no matter what happens, their means will remain the same.
Increases have been allowed in different commodities that the consumer has to buy. I maintain, and I think I am right, that these subsidies and these ceilings should have been maintained until goods became much more plentiful, because when you advance the price of one commodity you immediately in turn have to advance the price of another, and immediately after that you have to raise a man's wages to enable him to meet his increased cost of living
May I say in passing that the production of milk involves more drudgery than the production of any other commodity. The successful dairyman has always been the man with a family he could exploit. That is, the family milk the cows and produce the wealth, and their labour never was charged against the production of the milk. The government should maintain the ceiling and the subsidy so that these essential services to the nation may be carried on on a satisfactory basis. If you interfered with the ceiling or floor on fish, the same thing would happen to the fisherman. You would deprive him of his present income, out of which he would be compelled to pay for the expensive gear which he bought at war time prices.
The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) pointed out to the house last night that the fishermen's problems were never discussed in the way that the farmers' problems are. I can agree with him that there are more farmer members than fishermen members in this house, but I would be the last one in this house to forget the fishermen in my . constituency or any other part of Canada. He talked about the hard life and the long hours put in by the fishermen. I can agree with every word he said, because in the northern part of my constituency, where we have twenty hours of sunshine in the twenty-four, I have seen in the summer time-I did last summer-fishermen leave very early in the morning, and they were still dressing their catch by artificial light at night. This I am sure will compare favourably with the hours put in by the fishermen on the east coast. I do not think that the hardships and the risks taken by the fishermen on lake Winnipeg can be any less than those taken by the fishermen on either the east or west coast. Never a year passes but we read in our Manitoba papers that two or three fishermen have disappeared on an ice floe in their endeavours to feed a hungry world. I might say to hon. members that I have crossed the Atlantic at various times, both on modern liners and on tramp steamers, and never in all my experience have I seen rougher weather than that which can develop on lake Winnipeg. If we do not protect the ceilings and floors which have been established on fish, and at the same time see that the ceilings on the things that the fisherman has to buy are not destroyed, the risks he takes and the hardships he endures will bring him nothing.
I do not agree with my hon. friends to the right that ceilings should be taken off, but I want the government to be consistent, and not to advocate the maintenance of price controls on the floor of the house and to the
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

people of this country and then proceed to destroy those controls. Guaranteed ceilings and floors are more needed urgently to-day than they ever were in the history of Canada, and if the government breaks them it will be condemned for generations to come.
The government has a golden opportunity now to stabilize the economy of this country and prevent inflation. I say to them, if you want to build the new world that you have promised the people of Canada, don't fail them now. I ask this with but little hope; for the only difference I see between the government and the Tories on my right is that the Tories want to blow the top right off, and the Liberals want to do it gradually. I do hope and pray that they will maintain these ceilings and floors so that every Canadian, whether he be fisherman, farmer or worker, will be able to get his fair share of the national wealth. '

Mr. Speaker, first may I refer to the amendment and the subamendment. The amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) is as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the government's price ceiling policies with respect to farm products are discouraging production of needed food and imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's stabilization policies.
The C.C.F. amendment is:
This house is of the opinion that the government's policies of permitting recent unjustifiable increases in the prices of farm machinery and of steel have resulted in imposing on food producers and workers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the'government's price stabilization policies.
The subamendment has been very skilfully drawn. All of us can accept the view that in the light of the explanations so far given, the recent increase in the price of farm machinery is unjustifiable and unfair. But one thing which this subamendment does establish, as was made clear by the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Bryce) is that the C.C.F. do not believe that the farmers should receive any increase for their farm products. They have made their view perfectly plain in this regard.

I have just heard these terrible Tories referred to by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), and we did

not say anything. We listened. Now I am going to answer on behalf of this party, and I ask the same consideration-being always willing to answer questions-that was given to the hon. gentleman who preceded me.
When I listen to my hon. friends speaking over the radio in the province of Saskatchewan I notice that they do not say what they say here. They tell the farmer that he is not being fairly treated, that farm prices are lower in Canada than in the United States- the inference being that they support an increase in farm prices. But when they come into this house they move an amendment which can have only one effect, that of neutralizing the amendment introduced by the leader of the opposition, and striking a death-blow to the cause of any increase of farm prices in Canada. Apparently they do not believe that any increase of farm prices at the present time would be justified. If they have that view I know they are sincere; all I am trying to do is to make it perfectly clear that that is their point of view. One of my hon. friends said a moment ago that it was not. I propose to read from a very fine address given by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley), reported in Hansard of this session at page 867. The question of increased prices of farm implements was before the house. The leader of the opposition raised the question. He said the increase was unjustified, and hon. gentlemen in all parts of the house agreed with him and supported the condemnation he directed to the government in that regard.
The situation as to farm implements was this. There was an increase of $5 per ton in the price of steel in this country, as in the United States; but, the difference was this. In the United States-and this for my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) -the increase was given on the condition that the workers should receive an increase in wages. Now, sir, the leader of the opposition takes the stand, which I believe is also taken in all parts of the house, that conditions throughout the world to-day demand an extra production of farm products. One would scarcely think it necessary to establish that fact. Someone to my left has referred to what Mr. Hoover said recently on his return froiii abroad, and only within the last two days a general summation of the situation appeared in the Christian

Science Monitor, which shows what the people are facing in the different countries of Europe. I quote:
France-Average ration of meat for two meals is about two-thirds of an ounce. Potatoes are scarce.
Greece-With wheat supplies down to nine ounces a day per person, the nation is almost entirely dependent on the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration.
China-In Hunan province, known as the "rice bowl" of China, it is estimated that 7,000,000 persons of a population of 27,000,000 are approaching or are suffering starvation.
. Czechoslovakia-All foods except potatoes are rationed. Dairy products, fats and meats are short. Transportation difficulties are acute. Country gets one-seventh of its grain from UNRRA.
Hungary-Average daily ration, about 500 calories, is so low that medical officers assert it is responsible for 40 out of every 100 fatalities among children.
Italy-Two pounds of bread cost $4.50 on the "black market." Adequate "black market" meals cost $5.
Yugoslavia-Five million people rely entirely on UNRRA. In many places the only food available is three slices of bread a day.
Poland-Nine million bushels of grain will be needed within three months. Own grain stocks are running out. The nation is fast approaching the danger line of hunger.
Albania-Local grain stocks are running out. and about 57 per cent of the people now depend on UNRRA wheat and flour.
Belgium-Darker bread loaf has returned and "black market" is flourishing.
. Germany-Representative meal is a boiled potato, two spoonfuls of fish or hash, and dry bread. Potato supply is near exhaustion.
The situation there depicted undoubtedly calls for extra production, and how shall we obtain it? My hon. friends to my left have their own point of view in that regard. Australia found it necessary to raise the price of wheat; in other words, to raise the price which the farmer should receive, to the end that greater production be encouraged. Argentina is in the same position. The Canadian farmer is urged to produce essential foods to allay the starvation that stalks the world everywhere, and in no other country could there be such an increase in food supplies as there could be in Canada. In Russia, according to the New York Times two days ago, the present low standards of nutritional diet are such that even if agricultural production were expanded, the extra production would be needed at home. The United States can double its agricultural production, but this would necessitate a change in the whole economy of the. country, and several million people leaving the cities and going to the rural areas. In Australia and New Zealand, while there can be small increases, it is frankly admitted that there can be no material increase. Realizing conditions of famine in the world at large, in order to secure the extension

and expansion of production in wheat and other farm products at this time, our position is that prices of farm products should be increased, without in any way wishing to do as the hon. member for Selkirk has suggested, namely, to remove the price ceiling in its entirety. There is no such suggestion anywhere on the part of any official of this party. The only removal of the ceiling that we advocate is the removal of the ceiling on farm products so far as the present ceiling impedes production. Decontrol should only take place in other respects when the necessary supplies are available to assure a fair distribution. Speaking for myself alone, I say that if controls were removed altogether at this time I should be fearful of conditions everywhere in the country. On the other hand, much is made of the danger of inflation; but, may I add, nowhere has there ever been any serious inflation through increased prices, that are reasonable and fair, on farm products.
Take the situation in Canada to-day. Does the Minister of Finance say that there would be inflation if a fair and reasonable increase were allowed on the price of wheat and other farm products? He is fearful of inflation with increased farm prices. There was no fear of inflation in some of the social legislation which I supported, and which was brought in with the consent of hon. members in all parts of the house.
While the United States is endeavouring to encourage the production by the only means they know, the increase in price, which is also true of Australia and Argentina, here the policy is followed of refusing to face the situation which confronts this country. At this time the farmer, by reason not only of prices but also of unfairness of the income tax, is going on a strike in many parts of Canada, or he finds himself in a position where there is not the encouragement of production which there must be if there is to be the necessary production.
We believe that to establish extra production the first requisites are equity and security in farm prices. To remove the ceiling on farm prices to-day in order to bring them into line with world prices in no way requires the removal of the floor. No one suggests that. But we do say that with extraordinary and terrible conditions existing in the *world to-day, with famine stalking nineteen or twenty countries in a manner the like of which has not been seen in four hundred years, surely this is the time fo'r extraordinary measures to assure the production in the one country where production can be expanded and would be expanded if the government would give the lead.

With regard to farm costs, I realize that prices have gone up to some extent, but farm costs have also gone up. Only recently' R. J. Deachman, a well-known economist, wrote an article in which he took the 1939 prices as 100. In that article he pointed out that manufactured goods have risen 24-7 per cent; seeds, 77-4 per cent; feed, 61-8 per cent; gasoline, oil and grease, 23 per cent. I presume that is without the three-cent tax that should have been removed had there been any desire to encourage extra production on mechanized farms throughout the country. Building materials have risen 61-2 per cent; binder twine, 34-8 per cent, and farm labour 110-8 per cent.

I think it can be safely said from the statement made by the minister to-day that the farmers are going to get more than 81.55 a bushel for their wheat. When that happens let it be perfectly clear that it was not my hon. friends to the left, the C.C.F. party, that mobilized opinion in this country; it was the leader of the opposition who throughout the last year has been endeavouring to secure a fair and reasonable share of the national income for Canadian farmers..
With regard to income tax, I am not going to go into the various recommendations that were set forth in great detail by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at its meeting in London in January last. While by the recent changes in the income tax, a step was made in the right direction in order to secure the sale of the wheat that the farmers of Canada had on their hands, I suggest to the minister that at this session the basis of the assessment of income tax in so far as agriculture is concerned should be extended over the present period, and certainly over a five-year moving average. My hon. friends to the left have also frequently advocated this. I am in agreement with them on it. Allowance should be made for the labour of the farmer's wife, his sons and daughters in connection with farm production, because without these allowances being granted there is not the incentive that there should be to secure the necessary increase in production. I point out another difficulty in connection with the income tax. It has to do with hired help on the farm. A man comes to a farm and wants to get work. He refuses to work for the farmer who desires to deduct the income tax from his wages. While I realize that that condition cannot be rectified, nevertheless the fact remains that it is a factor.

Having regard to world conditions, no one in this house suggests that we should endeavour to take the world by the throat and to exact anything unfair. The government say that is what we would be doing if more than SI .55 a bushel for wheat were charged. They say that in selling below the world market price they do so in order to establish friendly relations in Europe and other parts of the world, so that when peace comes markets will be available. So that in reality we have a form of advertising, coupled with philanthropy, it is true, for which the farmers instead of all the people of Canada are asked to pay. As far as this party is concerned, it believes this. Sell wheat at whatever price you believe is reasonable, but do not saddle the farmer with any loss incidental to the advertising. That should be paid or assumed by the state.
As to the income tax, if the suggested changes are made and lowered rates imposed there will be greater incentive. I know there are those who say they believe in production for use rather than for profit, but they are the first to argue that, with the income tax as it is to-day and with the anomalies that exist, there is no incentive. By that very argument hon. gentlemen to my left show in effect how impossible it would be to change human nature under the influence of socialism. They say that the farmers will not produce because there is too little left over, because the income tax is too high. At the same time they say that there is a change in human nature, that mankind will accept the principle of production for use rather than profit.

It is important to those who hope to do the controlling. The members of this group believe that the individual citizens of this country should do their own planning and control themselves. This afternoon I heard the statement, "production for use and not for profit." Why that saying should be currently repeated, I do not know. Surely it is obvious that if a person is to produce something at a profit he must produce something useful. Otherwise there will be no profit. It is not up to any minority to tell the majority what they are to consume and how much. That is the affair of the individual, not of an organized minority.
The Liberals claim that they believe in the profit system, but they are destroying the profit system by taxation. In this connection I should like to read a letter which I received from a constitueht of mine, one of the best known agriculturists in the Lacombe district. I might say that the Lacombe district is one of the best farming districts in western Canada. It may interest the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to hear the contents of this letter. I am not sure, but I believe the writer is or was a supporter of the government; I do not think he is a supporter of mine. The letter is dated May 21, and reads:
Dear sir,
You will no doubt be somewhat surprised when you receive this letter from me and you no doubt receive many of the same nature from other people in this constituency along the same line.
I believe that in my business, which has extended over a period of almost thirty-eight years in this district, that I do have perhaps a better opportunity than most people to hear and know just what our farmers are doing and talking about, and I refer you especially to the present income tax law as regards our farmers.
I would like to point out to you and others who may be responsible for the present situation that during the last fall and this spring season of farm sales which I have conducted, there have been no less (and I think more) than 12 of our young and most successful farmers in the Bentley and Lacombe districts that have sold out and quit simply because they feel that the income tax is unjust and that they absolutely refuse to work 365 days in the year and then if they do happen to have a good crop, give the government anywhere from 25 to 40 per cent of it.
I know of others who are still staying on their farms, and men who a very short time ago were the largest feeders and raisers of live stock (cattle and hogs) that to-day are not feeding or raising a single head of live stock. They say that they are not going to buy feeders, work every day, Sunday as well as week days, snow or blow, cold and wet and then if they are lucky enough to make a few dollars give most of it to the government for income tax.
IMr. Jaques.l
Others that I know are quitting and hiring all the work done on the farm. I am of the opinion that the farmers of this district are no different from the farmers all over Canada. Most of them feel that when they have paid their municipal, school, social service and many other indirect taxes they have done enough tax paying. They all feel that they are not getting a fair and equitable deal regarding their income tax. They talk something like this. That it is nowhere near fair to tax them plenty when they are fortunate enough to get a good crop as well as price, and then when they are hailed, froze or dried out and get no crop, there is no recompense.
Now then, Mr. Jaques, you can do as you please about ivhat I have written. Do something about it or throw this into the wastepaper basket. But I am telling you and those who are in power at Ottawa that they have got to do something about this whole business, or we are not going to have any good farmers left in this district.
That letter is signed by Mr. C. F. Damron, one of the best known agriculturists in western Canada. There is no man with a sounder knowledge of farming than Mr. Damron and there are no better farming districts -I doubt if there are any as good in the whole of western Canada-than Lacombe and Bentley. That is the condition of the farmers there. While the socialists would, I suppose, make profits a criminal offence, the Liberals are making profits impossible through taxation, and under the orthodox system of finance there is no alternative. As I said when I started, they are all going the same road; they are all going the same place. The only quarrel is over who shall do the planning and who shall do the controlling.
I have heard something about inflation. What is the cure, and the only cure for inflation? It is production. Why should we not have more production? Because the producers in the first place are discouraged by taxation, or they are frightened by what more controls may be in store for them. They are uncertain; they do not like to go ahead and start things when they cannot see the end of their ventures.
I would not, of course, advocate the complete removal of controls, but as a general policy I am all in favour of doing away with controls as quickly as may be possible. I believe in free enterprise. There are only two methods of production. There is persuasion, and there is compulsion-it is one or the other. So far we have always had production by persuasion, and under that system we have not only produced enough for everybody but we have actually had overproduction. It is not really a matter of production. We have solved that problem. We shall have to solve the problem of consumption, and that cannot be done by the

old price system, by orthodox finance and orthodox economics. As I said, the Liberals and Conservatives would plan and control by taxation, while the socialists would have planned production, which, of course, in the end means planned scarcity. That is the history in those countries where socialism has really been tried out.
I am familiar with one of the choicest and most desirable parts of western Canada. I refer to the Fraser valley in British Columbia, and I see that the member of Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) is in his seat. I have lived in the valley and I am fairly well familiar with conditions there. It is one of the garden spots of the world. At the present time I believe the farmers there are prosperous. I am glad to say that they have done well, but for many years before the war they were certainly in a depressed condition. I have close relations who are producing milk in the Fraser valley and I had many conversations with them before the war. They depend, of course, upon the Vancouver market to sell their whole milk. Their trouble before the war was this, *that although the market and the demand for milk was there, the demand was not effective because it was not supported by money. The Fraser valley milk producers' association had the idea that if they could only get 100 per cent of the retail market they could raise the price of milk by keeping a certain amount of it off the market. In other words, they could raise the price by making milk more scarce. I used to tell them:	If you could do that,
apart from the moral question involved, you would do two things at once. If you succeeded in raising retail prices under these conditions, you would at once stimulate the production of milk in the valley, but you would also lower the sales of milk because, although you raise the price, you do nothing to increase the effective purchasing power of the people to pay the extra price, and what would happen would be this. You would increase the supply of milk, but much of it would go into the milk factories and be sold on the market in the can. There is no profit for them selling milk in the can; their profit is in selling raw milk over the retail counter. But since the war they have done very well for the simple reason that there has been a great increase in the population of Vancouver. I do not know the figures, but there has been a very great increase in Vancouver's population, and of course an enormous increase in payrolls, so that there is more money in the hands of the people. The reason why these farmers in the Fraser valley have done well is simply that they have sold most
of the milk in the raw state over the retail counter because the people want the raw milk and have money to pay for it.
The reason I mention this is that the milk subsidy is to be taken off. I believe that is a great mistake. What we have to do is to stimulate production and the only real way to stimulate production is to stimulate consumption. We should finance consumption, and then production will finance itself. The milk subsidy-and there were others-was a direct application of a social credit principle, and that is the direct financing of consumption. It was done in Great Britain during the war to an enormous extent; I have not the exact figures but I believe it was something like one billion dollars a year. I understand that this subsidy is to be removed. I think that is a great mistake. If we take care of consumption, production will take care of itself.
Conditions after this war have been compared with conditions after the last war. In fact I heard an hon. member contradict himself: he pointed to conditions in 1919 as an illustration of the terrors of inflation, and later on in his speech he said that 1919 and 1920 were the only years when the farmer got a just reward. According to that, you can have a just reward only under inflation. Then he blamed on inflation-or at least I so understood him'-the depression which followed those good years. It was nothing of the kind. As I remember it-and I was farming at the time; in fact I have been farming since 1901, and that is a considerable time-after the last war there was an extraordinary recovery. In a. year, or perhaps two years, the world seemed to have recovered. There was no talk of starvation; there was no talk of famine; there was plenty, and very soon there was more than plenty; in fact it was said that there was over-production.
Why have we .the opposite conditions today? We talk about famine and starvation. You cannot get any goods. You go to a store to buy even such a thing as a shirt and you cannot get it. In those days there was plenty of goods but no money; in these days there is money but no goods. I say that both those conditions are artificial, and I believe they are deliberately brought about, through planning. What we are doing with regard to food is, we are entrusting the control of the world's food to the hands of very few people. I hear complaints and criticisms of such institutions as the grain exchange. Some people think it would be better and safer to do away with such bodies and place the control under a board; in other words, in the hands of a few people. To my mind that is a most dangerous

proposal. It is a terrible proposal. Already we see some of the consequences of these controls; certain countries are being threatened with starvation if they do not toe the line. What we are coming to is world dictatorship, world tyranny through the control of the world's food. If that is the " new order," for heaven's sake let us keep to the old. World control or world planning, with the systems of coupons and rationing, means world slavery. I will say this, that only the crook demands and only the craven desires security at the price of freedom.

The responsibility for having broken the price ceiling structure cannot be placed anywhere except on the shoulders of the government. I clearly remember listen-1 ing to the speeches of the candidates of the party opposite during the last election. Their expressed policy was one of maintaining price ceilings in fairness to all. They held out promises of full employment, good wages and fair prices, things which we could all well support. They did not intimate that in western Canada the price of gasoline would go up two cents a gallon. They did not give us any warning that the price of paper, textiles and millinery, steel products and so forth would all go up in price inside of one year. They were elected in good faith on their platform of maintaining a stabilized price structure. That was in June. 1945.
There is another angle which has to be considered before we go further, namely, the injustices which have cropped up or which are now in the present ceiling policy of the government. In many cases these are injustices which started five years ago. It is not something that has cropped up overnight. When the price freezing order was put on in 1941, prices and wages were frozen at levels which, in many instances, were not adequate. No one will say that in 1941 the price of farm products was the right price. According to the bureau of statistics, in 1941 the average price of wheat, which is a staple product of the west, was only fifty-five cents a bushel. That is the average of all grades. No one will say that that was a fair price. If one wants to go into wages he will find that many of them were far below standard, and yet evidently it was accepted by the government that the price which obtained in 1941, when the order was put in, was the correct price for everybody. Very little effort was made in the first year or two to make adjustments where adjustments wrere needed. That is a matter of history.
The hon. member to my right brought up to-day the question of the increase in the price of wheat. He said that if a price increase is allowed it will not be because of the C.C.F. group but because of the- action of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). I cannot understand how an hon. member can make that statement when he knows the history of prices. Let me take him back to 1943. At that time the present leader of the opposition was not in the house. I am doubtful whether he then owed allegiance to the party which he is now leading. That, of course, does not matter. In 1943 four by-elections were held in this country. Shortly before they were held a delegation of four hundred farmers from western Canada, practically all of them from Saskatchewan, came to interview the government in an effort to have the initial price of wheat raised to at least $1 a bushel. That is all past history. We know that the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is
credited with having said that if four hundred farmers could afford to come all the way from Saskatchewan to Ottawa as a delegation they did not need a price increase very badly, and they were not very successful at the time. As I say, four by-elections were held in 1943. In the riding of Selkirk the hon. member who now represents that riding in this house, was elected. In Humboldt the hon. member who now represents that riding in the house was elected by an overwhelming majority. That did more to raise the price of wheat than all the delegations that had come here prior to that time. - In other words, what was it that caused the price to jump not to $1 but to $125 a bushel? It was because the people of the west expressed themselves emphatically at the polls in Selkirk and Humboldt, and they did so by voting for C.C.F. candidates.

subsubtopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: We did not change our name, as you did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Would my hon. friend mind moving the adjournment of the debate, in order that I may make a motion before six o'clock, or is he finished now?

subsubtopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Very well; I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned. BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext: That the provision of standing order 28 in relation to Mr. Speaker leaving the chair without question put for the house to go into committee of supply be suspended for the sitting on Thursday, May 23, 1946

subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext: I understand this is to come within the rules and make it possible to continue this debate to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext: Speaking for this party, we are entirely in favour of this procedure. Might I ask if some consideration has been given to whether or not this will pass if it is protested?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext: Unless there is unanimous consent we cannot pass it.

subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext: Does it require unanimous consent to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext: No; just now.

subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext:
Then you have our
consent.

subsubtopic: SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28
speechtext: And you have the consent of this group also.

Motion agreed to.

Thursday, May 23, 1946.
